contentHtml:
GLOBAL—Spain and 20 countries have joined the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF in launching a global campaign to reduce obesity prevalence by 5% by 2030, strengthening international efforts to prevent and manage the growing public health challenge.

The initiative, titled Bending the Curve by 2030, brings together Spain and 20 countries participating in WHO’s Acceleration Plan to Stop Obesity.

These include Bahrain, Barbados, Botswana, Brazil, Brunei Darussalam, Egypt, Eswatini, Ireland, Jordan, Malaysia, Mauritius, Mexico, Panama, the Philippines, Portugal, Seychelles, Slovenia, South Africa, Thailand and Uruguay.

The participating governments have committed to accelerating obesity prevention, improving early intervention and expanding access to treatment and care.

The campaign also seeks to strengthen national policies that address the environmental and social factors contributing to obesity.

Rising global obesity burden

More than one billion people worldwide are living with obesity, which now affects approximately one in seven people.

Since 1990, obesity prevalence has more than doubled among adults and quadrupled among adolescents.

In 2025, obesity also overtook underweight as the most common form of malnutrition among children and adolescents aged 5 to 19.

WHO classifies obesity as a form of malnutrition and a chronic, complex disease associated with an increased risk of noncommunicable diseases, including cardiovascular conditions, diabetes and certain cancers.

“Obesity is one of the defining public health challenges of our time, but its continued rise is not inevitable,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.

He commended governments for committing to healthier environments, stronger child protection measures and improved access to obesity treatment and support.

Policy priorities and healthcare delivery

The global campaign identifies three priorities: preventing overweight and obesity across populations, identifying and supporting people at higher risk through early intervention, and expanding access to timely, effective and affordable treatment.

Participating countries are encouraged to implement evidence-based measures, including breastfeeding support, appropriate complementary feeding, healthier school environments and taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages.

Other interventions include front-of-pack nutrition labelling, restrictions on marketing unhealthy foods to children and policies that encourage physical activity.

The initiative also calls for stronger obesity prevention and management within primary healthcare systems, including access to pharmacological treatment where clinically appropriate.

For healthcare systems, these measures have implications for primary care capacity, preventive health financing, nutrition policies and access to obesity medicines.

 They also create opportunities for governments to strengthen collaboration between healthcare providers, food manufacturers, schools and public health agencies.

The campaign further emphasises the involvement of people living with obesity in designing policies and healthcare services, recognising their role in shaping effective interventions.

Mónica García Gómez, Spain’s Minister of Health, said the participating countries aim to reduce childhood obesity prevalence by 5% by 2030, with success depending on policies reaching schools, communities and families facing barriers to healthier environments.

International collaboration and early progress

WHO and UNICEF have reported emerging data from some countries indicating potential early declines in obesity prevalence.

The organisations are working with governments and partners to identify the factors behind these trends and assess how successful interventions can be replicated.

Dr Karen Sealey, a physician from Trinidad and Tobago, international health consultant and board member of the World Obesity Federation who lives with obesity, said discussions at the Global Obesity Summit and Stocktaking in Madrid highlighted the need for stronger collaboration.

Drawing on her experience as a patient and international health consultant, she emphasized that coordinated efforts involving WHO, UNICEF, and the World Obesity Federation are essential to improving healthcare responses and the lives of people living with obesity.
